en: Preface to the *Shoulengyan Jing Zhizhang Shu* (Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: Pointing at the Palm):

In the autumn of the Year of Dingmao, while attending upon the Venerable Elder [Zhaocheng] at Yiguang Temple to listen to his lectures on the *Zhengmo* (The Correct Pulse), I encountered points of contradiction within the commentary.
On each occasion, I was graced by his clarifications and was shown his own personal insights. He once spoke of composing a commentary himself, though he had not yet found the leisure to do so.
Subsequently, the period of precepts concluded. In this year, Gengwu, the Elder performed the ritual of returning from the altar and retired to Yiguang, who moved to Jiaxing.
I also requested leave to visit my teacher in my hometown; on my way back, I passed through Xishan and took up residence among the mountain clouds.
As time slipped by and the years passed, we reached the winter of Xinwei, when the Elder was appointed to preside over the seat at Xiangjie. The following year was Renshen.
In the summer, I came from Xuoyun to pay my respects to the Elder. He had composed a preface for a lecture; I was filled with joy beyond measure, as it now accorded with what he had said in the past.
The following year, in the spring of the Guiyou year, the period for the commencement of the retreat began. The ritual protocols were transmitted and the new preface was lectured upon.

At that time, I served as his right-hand assistant and listened by his side, receiving much inspiration. In the following year, the Jiaxu year, I requested that the Elder preside over the completion of the dharma-assembly.

Entering the city to perform his ministry, he entrusted me with the summer retreat and the task of lecturing. During that time, I would unroll the scroll to contemplate its meaning and present it to the assembly each day to expound upon it.
Comparing it with previous commentaries, I found it to possess an entirely new character. I reflect privately that, should one wish to explore rare treasures, [one must seek this work].
He had to travel across the vast ocean; consequently, he suspended his lectures, observed the *jinzu* (retreat) vow, and paid homage to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* while perusing the *Dragon Canon*.

As the seasons alternated between cold and heat, his work on the canon reached three cycles. Although his prostrations before the sutras were complete, his reading of the entire canon was not yet finished.

Before long, he was pressed by the command to transport grain along the canal; it was not until the end of the year that he returned to await the following year. On an auspicious day in the first month of the year Wuyin, the Elder [the Master] together with two...
Preface: Entrusted by the various mountain monasteries and lay patrons, I was charged with acting as a provisional abbot to manage the affairs of the Venerable’s quarters.

I reflected that it was like a mosquito attempting to carry Mount Tai; my strength was insufficient for such a task. Nevertheless, the Master’s command was difficult to refuse, and so I accepted it out of necessity.

From this point on, the Elder entered the city and established a three-year period of formal lectures at Jiayu Monastery, which has now concluded. I reflect deeply that while the original draft of this preface was rudimentary, I have now revised it.

The embellishments have not yet been finalized; it is necessary to extract what is beneficial for the present and future and add deletions and supplements. For this reason, I have again exhausted my mental faculties and once more worn through the bamboo slips [of the *Analects*].

Although my duties are numerous, I treat this work as urgent; though my years are not yet full, I have already completed more than half of the revisions. This was not merely due to the addition of spiritual inspiration, but also because I relied upon the grace of the Sage.
As I came to the mountain on business, he commanded me to examine and collate the text. I replied: "If one wishes to distinguish and correct errors, one must return..."
The merit of scholarly discourse must be pursued. Thus, from the time of opening this text until the day of its formal exposition, I have exhaustively investigated its contents.

Where there were occasional discrepancies in characters or phrases, I did not fail to correct them. However, regarding the ancient accounts and scriptural citations cited within the commentary, many points remained doubtful and lacked definitive evidence;
for this reason, I searched through a multitude of records and privately consulted those of broad learning. Before a year had passed—
This has been compiled as a volume to assist in the circulation of the commentary on the sutra. It is titled *The Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:

A Manual for the Hand and the Meaning of the Matter*. This work employs historical accounts from ancient authorities and phrasing worthy of emulation from various scriptures to corroborate the principles established in the present commentary.
Thus, the commentary may be fully elucidated, and the sutra will be free from doubt or obstruction. May its influence extend far and wide.
From this point on, for those who ascend from the low ground, I shall provide a modest aid.
This concludes the "General Introduction" to the *Shou Lengyan Jing Zhizhang Shu* (Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
Pointing to the Palm).

Someone asked about the principles of the Di sacrifice. The Master said, "I do not know them. He continued, "One who knows these principles, when it comes to governing the world, is it any different from pointing at something here?
As he spoke, he pointed to his palm. This expresses that [the task] is clear and easy. (See *Analects*, Part I.)

"Do not find fault with me," said the Master. "As for Yu, I have no grounds for finding fault. The commentary states: *Jian* (間) means a crack or fissure; it refers to pointing out such flaws in order to criticize them.
This is found in the first part of the *Analects*.
The phrase "hanging one and missing ten" appears in the *New Gazetteer of Putuo*, meaning that what has been selected is meager while what has been omitted is vast.
The rising sun first shines upon the high mountains.
The *Avataṃsaka* states: "For example, when the sun rises, it first illuminates the great high mountains such as Mount Sumeru. The Tathāgata is likewise;

having perfected the wheel of wisdom of the boundless Dharma-realm, he constantly emits the unimpeded light of wisdom, first illuminating the great mountain kings such as the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. This appears in the fiftieth fascicle.
In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, Kāśyapa reproaches himself, saying: "Why have we eternally severed our roots? Regarding this Mahāyāna, we are like ruined seeds.
The commentary explains: "Ruined seeds" refers to seeds that have already been destroyed and are incapable of sprouting; [the same applies to] the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), which are like ashes.

When the body is extinguished, the wisdom [of those] who are unable to generate the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna is likewise so. Now, this commentary takes the metaphor of those of inferior, middling, and small capacities;
the Black Mountains are briefly illuminated.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Next, the Tathāgata’s wheel of wisdom illuminates the Black Mountains; next, it illuminates the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who are like those who feel an elephant and obtain only a semblance of it.
The thirty-second fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "For example, there was a king who told a great minister to assemble many blind men."
He brought an elephant to show them. Then those blind men each felt it with their hands. The king called the blind men one by one and asked them, "What is the elephant like?
The one who had touched its tusks said, "The shape of the elephant is like the root of a radish. The one who had touched its ears...
One who touches its head says the elephant is like a winnowing basket; one who touches its trunk says it is like a stone; one who touches its feet says it is like a pestle;
one who touches its back says it is like a mortar; one who touches its spine says it is like a bed; and one who touches its belly [says it is like a wall].

One who touches its head says the elephant is like a jar; one who touches its tail says the elephant is like a rope. Good son, these blind men do not describe the actual substance of the elephant, yet it is not that they do not describe it at all.

If all these various characteristics are not the elephant itself, and there is no other elephant apart from them, then we now take this [description] to serve as a metaphor for the various schools. Their divergent theories are manifold and confused, yet they only capture a semblance of the truth.
Regarding this meaning,
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle fourteen, states:
"It is like a person born blind who does not know the color of milk and asks another, 'What is the color of milk?'"
"What is the color like? The other replied, "The color is white, like a conch shell. The blind man asked again, "Is this milk-colored [object] like the sound of a conch shell?
He replied, "No. He asked again, "What is the color of the conch shell like? He replied, "It is like rice powder.
The blind man asked again, "Is the color of the milk as soft as rice powder? And what is rice powder like?"
[The questioner] asks what it resembles. He replies, "It is like snow or rain. The blind man asks again, "Is that rice flour as cold as snow?
[The questioner] asks what the snow resembles. He replies, "It is like a white crane.

Although this person born blind has heard these four kinds of analogies, he is ultimately unable to recognize the true color of the milk. These non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are also just like this; they ultimately...

One can thereby attain the permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Now, this commentary adopts these [terms] as metaphors for the various schools; yet they possess only verbal explanations and lack any true meaning, leading to doubt.
The fox is a cunning beast whose nature is full of doubt. When crossing a frozen river in winter, it moves forward while listening;

if there is no sound of water flowing beneath the ice, it proceeds, but if there is a sound, it retreats. Because its advancing and retreating are inconsistent, it serves as a metaphor for the doubter who beholds the Vajra Mind-Seal.
"When the phoenix’s offspring is first born, it desires to soar above the clouds.
The *Yilin* says: "The phoenix has ten offspring; they share one nest and one mother. It also says: "The phoenix gave birth to five chicks, who grew up in the southern suburb.
Song Yu addressed King Xiang of Chu, saying: "The phoenix soars upward to nine thousand *zhang*, transcending the clouds and mists, bearing the azure sky..."
O Heaven! A gull on the fence—how could it measure the height of heaven and earth? See the *Jiànshìlèi fù* (Rhyme-prose on the Classification of Affairs).
The *Dǐngxiǎng* says: "Tàijiǎ overthrew the statutes and precedents of Tāng; Yíyǐn banished him to Tóng. After three years, Tàijǐa..."

Jia repented his transgressions, lamenting and reforming himself. The commentary states: "Diānfù" means overturned and brought into disorder; "diǎn xíng" refers to the constant laws. "Tóngtāng" is the location of his tomb.
"Āi" means to rectify, or to trim grass—to cut it down. This likely signifies the intent to sever [the past] and begin anew, as seen in the "Wànzhāng" chapter.
Now, in this commentary, I have changed "xíng" to "yíng," taking the established laws of the former sages as a model for later students.

At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the youth Sudhana, saying:
"Good son, if you wish to accomplish the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), you should resolutely seek a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Good son, in seeking a spiritual friend..."
Do not give rise to weariness or indolence. Upon seeing a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), do not feel complacency or satisfaction.
You should comply with all the instructions of the spiritual friend. Regarding all the skillful means of the spiritual friend, do not look for faults.
Son of good family, to the south of here, there is a land called Uttarakuru. In that land, there is a mountain named Sumeru. Therein...
“There is a bhikṣu named Meghaśrī. You should go and ask him: ‘How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct? How does he cultivate the bodhisattva conduct? ... [and so on] ... up to:
‘How does one quickly attain the fulfillment of the conduct of Samantabhadra? Bhikṣu Meghaśrī will explain this for you.
When the youth Sudhana heard these words, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated himself, touching his head to the ground in salutation.
He circumambulated [the Buddha] countless times, gazing up at him with earnest devotion and weeping tears of sorrow. Then, taking his leave, he traveled south toward the land of Sukhāvatī.
Proceeding in this manner, he passed through more than one hundred and ten cities and paid homage to fifty-three true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Finally, within the pore-pores of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, he successively attained the [vows and practices of] Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
He is equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas regarding the ocean of all practices and vows, even unto inconceivable liberation and mastery;
these are all entirely identical. This is seen in detail in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicles 62 through 80.

The Dharma accomplishes all things through its subtle transformations; as the *Commentary on the Appended Phrases* of the *Book of Changes* states: "The transformations of Heaven and Earth accomplish the myriad things subtly and completely, leaving none out.
Now, by categorizing and analyzing these points in detail according to the capacities of beings, we adopt the principle of that subtle accomplishment of Heaven and Earth.
Regarding the saying that "eating does not satisfy":

after the Great Master Huineng of the Sixth Generation had his mind certified and received the robe at Huangmei during the midnight transmission, he traveled by stages until he arrived at Faxing Temple in Guangzhou.
There, he encountered Dharma Master Yinzong lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, who invited him to take the seat of honor and questioned him.

He interrogated [the Master] on the profound meaning; his words were concise yet the principles were appropriate, transcending mere literary expression. The following day, Magistrate Wei requested further instruction.
The Master ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying: "Everyone, with a pure mind, recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, O virtuous friends, the wisdom of Bodhi and Prajñā is inherently possessed by all people of the world; it is only because the mind is deluded that one is unable [to realize it]."
To awaken on one's own, one must rely upon a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to guide one toward the realization of one’s own nature.
I shall now expound for you the Dharma of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, so that each of you may attain wisdom. Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall speak for you.

Spiritual friends, worldly people spend their days reciting the name of *prajñā* with their mouths, yet they do not recognize the *prajñā* of their own nature; it is just like describing the taste of food.

One will remain unsatisfied; though the mouth speaks only of emptiness, one shall not perceive one's nature for ten thousand kalpas, and in the end it will be of no benefit. See this in detail in the *Dharmapada Sūtra* (The Platform Sutra).
To constantly count others' wealth while remaining poor.

Once there was a man in dire straits who found a discarded document by the roadside. Upon seeing the various figures recorded therein—of fields, gardens, palaces, gold, silks, rice, and millet—he rejoiced beyond his wildest expectations and declared himself a man of immense wealth.
He failed to realize that while he was counting another’s treasures, they had no connection whatsoever to himself.
This is what is meant by the saying: "Though one knows that mind is itself Buddha, it is clear that the mind is not the Buddha. Thus it is seen.
The *Tadashu Shō* states:
"In the Indic language, the regions of Chu, Xia, Qin, and Luo are called Zhonghua (Central China). They are also called Huaxia and Zhongxia. The lands of Huainan and Chu are not [part of this]."

The dialects of the Central Kingdom (Zhōngguó) differ from those of Chǔ and Xià in their phonology and the weight of their intonations when calling out names. Now, the Sanskrit language of the Western Regions bears a resemblance to this;

for it is likely that Central India corresponds to the Central Kingdom, while the other four regions correspond to the land of Chǔ. This is seen in the *Huayan xuantan* (Prolegomena to the Avataṃsaka).

The "holy teachings of this region" referred to here are the teachings of Confucius. They are called "jīng" (classics), as in the designation of the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Yì*, *Lǐ*, and *Chūnqiū* as the Five Classics (*wǔ jīng*).
The *Sūtra* (Sanskrit: *sūtra*) belongs to the holy teachings of the Western Regions; therefore, it is also translated as "jīng. This is seen in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
