"Those who take human life die and enter hell; if they are born among humans, their lifespan is short. You must depart immediately; you need not remain here.
Śamatha then departed from the country himself. When the king’s army arrived at the gate again, the evil Māra Pāpīyān assumed the form of a naked man and called out, "Open the gate quickly!
The Śākyas opened the gate. The king said, "Since the Śākya clan is so numerous, bury them all."
He ordered his footmen to have the wild elephant trample them to death. He selected five hundred Śākya women and took them to the place where the kings were.
At that time, Mahānāman requested a boon from the king, and the king immediately granted it. Mahānāman said, "I shall now submerge myself in the water;
for as long as it takes me to emerge, let all the Śākyas escape as they please. Once I have emerged from the water, kill them all. The king replied, "Very well," and immediately—
He entered the bottom of the water and tied his hair to the roots of a tree, thereby ending his own life. The Śākyas of the city rushed to the four gates;
the King told his ministers, "Mahānāma’s father has not emerged until now. He immediately entered the water and found that he was already dead.
The King felt remorse in his heart, thinking, "My maternal grandfather has now passed away solely because of his attachment to his kinsmen. Had he known this earlier..."
He never engaged in offensive warfare, yet nine million nine hundred and ninety thousand people were killed and scattered; their blood flowed until it formed a river.
After the army had departed, the Buddha, together with the bhikṣus, went to Kapilavastu. Arriving at the eastern gate, he saw smoke and fire blazing within the city gates.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus, "In the past, I preached the Dharma here among these people, but now there are no inhabitants."
He did not return again, but went back to the Jeta Grove and informed the bhikṣus: "Seven days from now, King Pūru and his army shall all be utterly destroyed.
When the king heard this, he was terrified. A brahmin said, "Both within and without, there is no dust; let the king enjoy himself.
The king sent men to count [the days] until the morning of the seventh day. The king was greatly rejoiced and led his various troops and attendants.
The women went to the banks of the Ajiravatī River to hold a banquet together. Suddenly, a great thunderclap resounded;

untimely clouds arose, and a violent wind and torrential rain broke out, causing injury, destruction, and drowning until everyone was gone at once. King Śreṇiya entered the Avīci Hell, and furthermore, there was a celestial fire.
The palace buildings were set ablaze and consumed. A bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying, "For what reason have these Śākyas now encountered such suffering?

The Buddha said, "In the past, within the city of Rājagṛha, there was a fishing village. At that time, the world suffered from famine; people ate the roots of plants, and one measure of gold was traded for one measure of rice.
In a great pond in the village, fish were exceedingly abundant. The people caught and ate them. There were two kinds of fish: the first..."
One was named Kṣudraka and the other was named Bahujihva. They said to one another, "We are aquatic creatures who do not dwell on dry land, yet these people all come to devour us.
In that village there was a young boy about eight years old; although he did not catch fish, he would rejoice whenever he saw them.
The people of Rājagṛha village are now the Śākyas. The Kṣudraka fish were the [Śākya] Mallas.
King Li was he. The talkative fish was the ascetic Brahmin who delighted in austerities. The child who saw the fish and laughed is now I.
Because of the sin of catching that fish, I suffered the torments of hell for incalculable eons; today, facing him, I see him and laugh with joy.

Now I suffer from a headache, as if being crushed by a stone. [This is recorded in] the *Śākyamuni-pāpavinirmukti-sūtra*, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, and the *Lüyi xiang* (Various Phenomena of the Sūtras and Vinaya).
Regarding the three full difficulties of Vajragarbha:

The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if all sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning, for what reason do they still possess all forms of ignorance?
If this ignorance has existed in sentient beings from the beginning, by what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata further declare that they have been Buddhas from the very beginning?
That ordinary beings throughout the ten directions have fundamentally realized the Buddha-way, yet subsequently give rise to ignorance? All...
"When will the Tathāgata again give rise to all afflictions? At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"Good son, it is like a phantom cataract falsely perceiving flowers in the sky. If the phantom cataract is removed, one cannot say, 'This cataract has been extinguished;
when will all such cataracts arise again? Why is this? Because the two phenomena of the cataract and the flowers [are non-existent]."
Because they exist in mutual dependence. It is also like the extinction of flowers in the sky; one cannot say that empty space will ever again give rise to flowers.
Why? Because space originally has no flowers; it is not subject to arising or ceasing.

Birth-and-death and nirvana are likewise subject to arising and ceasing, whereas the wondrous, perfect enlightenment is free from the cataracts of such flowers. Good son, it is like refining gold ore: the gold is not created by the refining.
It exists. Once it has already become gold, it is no longer treated as ore; even after an infinite period of time, the nature of the gold does not perish.
One should not say that it was originally unaccomplished. The Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is also like this, O son of good family. All Tathāgatas...

The wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind is fundamentally devoid of both bodhi and nirvana; it is likewise devoid of attaining Buddhahood or not attaining Buddhahood, and devoid of delusory saṃsāra or non-saṃsāra.
Good son, any conceptualization involving effort arises from the state of having a mind;

these are all the vaporous conditions of delusive thoughts regarding the six sense-objects, not the true essence of the mind, being like flowers in the sky. To employ such conceptualization to discern—

Within the realm of the Buddha, it is like empty flowers further producing empty fruits; to engage in such successive deluded imaginings is impossible. This is seen in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, which exposes such forced interpretations.
Mencius said: "What I dislike about those who claim to be wise is their artificiality. If one were truly wise, it would be like Yu’s management of the waters;
then there would be nothing to dislike in his wisdom. Yu’s management of the waters consisted of acting where there was nothing to act upon.
If the wise man also acts where there is nothing to act upon, then his wisdom would indeed be great. The commentary states: "The principles of the world are originally all..."
Those who are clever and compliant, and whose minds are sharp, strive to engage in forced interpretation and thereby miss the point.
When Yu regulated the waters, he followed their natural course and guided them; he never used his private ingenuity to force an artificial path.
Thus, the water attained its inherent nature of flowing downward and did no harm. This is seen in the "Lilou" chapter.
Regarding the region of Sangjian and Puchang, the "Record of Music" (*Yueji*) chapter of the *Liji* states: "The music of Sangjian and Puchang is the music of a ruined state. The commentary notes:
"Sangjian and Puchang were locations in the territory of Wei; it refers to the area between the Sanglin groves on the banks of the Puchuan River. The *Shiji* further records that Lord Ling of Wei...
While visiting Jin, he stayed at Puchang. At night, he heard the sound of a lute. He summoned Shi Juan to listen to it and transcribe it.
Upon arriving in Jin, he ordered Juan to perform it for Duke Ping. Master Kuang said, "This is the seductive music of Shi Yan.
When King Wu attacked Zhou, Shi Yan threw himself into the Puchuan River and died. Therefore, hearing this sound must be upon the banks of the Puchuan."

When Cook Ding was disassembling an ox for Lord Wen Hui, his hand met with nothing but the natural seams, his shoulder leaned against nothing but the joints, and his foot trod upon nothing but the spaces between the bones. He never encountered the tough sinews or knotted ligaments.
Wherever his knee was caught, there came a *hu* sound; as he applied the blade, there was a *hua* sound—none of which failed to accord with music.
It matched the dance of Sanglin and hit the rhythm of the Jingshou. Lord Wenhui said, "Aha! How excellent! Has the skill reached such a height?"
Pao Ding set down his knife and replied, "What Your Servant delights in is the Way; it goes beyond mere skill.
When I first began to butcher oxen, there was nothing before my eyes but the ox. Three years later, I no longer saw the ox as a whole."
At this present time, my spiritual encounter with the Way is such that I do not rely on the eyes to see. Each official knows when to stop, yet the spirit desires to act.
Relying upon the natural order (*tianli*), I cleave through the great cavities and guide [the blade] through the great apertures, following what is inherently so.

Even the sinews, ligaments, and connective tissues of bone and flesh have never obstructed me, let alone large bones. The commentary states: "One employs the knife by following the natural principle, proceeding from the bone and flesh."
Even in these minor points of contact, no discordance is seen; how much less could there be the obstruction of "great bones"?
See the "Nourishing the Lord of Life" chapter in the Inner Chapters of the *Zhuangzi*.
"To travel a long distance begins from near at hand;
to ascend a height begins from below," as stated in the *Zhongyong*. The commentary says: "The Way of the gentleman proceeds in orderly sequence.
To fully realize one's nature and reach the destiny of life must be rooted in human relations and daily affairs."

The constant principle of ordering one’s position and nourishing all things within the harmony of the Mean must necessarily be grounded in the moments of hiddenness, subtlety, solitude, and privacy. Such is the way of the gentleman.
It is like traveling a great distance: one must begin from what is near; it is like ascending a high mountain: one must begin from a low place.
How can those who seek the Way fail to know what they should apply themselves to?
"Knowing what comes first and what comes last brings one close to the Way.
The *Great Learning* says: "Things have their roots and branches; affairs have their beginnings and ends. To know what comes first and what comes last is to be near the Way. The commentary states:

"The brightening of one's virtue (*mingde*) and the transforming of the people (*xinmin*) are both 'things. However, one must first brighten one's virtue before one can transform the people. Things do not lack a root."
The end? To know where to stop and to be able to attain [the goal] are both matters of practice. However, one must first know where to stop before one can attain it.
Does a matter not have a beginning and an end? The beginning is what comes first; the end is what follows last. If one understands this sequence of priority, then one’s progress will be orderly;
naturally, one proceeds from the root to the branches, and from the beginning to the conclusion. Thus, regarding the *Great Learning*—
"The Way is not far off.
This was not for a swordsman;
had it been, he would not have offered the sword. When Chan Master Linji Yixuan of Zhinzhou arrived at Fenglin, Fenglin said, "May I ask you a question?"
The Master said, "How can you carve flesh to create a sore? Lin said, "The sea moon is clear and shadowless; the roaming fish alone is deluded.
The Master said, "If the sea moon has no shadow, how can the roaming fish be deluded? Lin said, "Observing the wind, one knows the waves arise; gazing at the water, the wild sail drifts.
The Master said, "The solitary moon shines alone as mountains and rivers fall silent; a single long cry resounds, and heaven and earth turn autumnal."
Lin said, "Let Zhang wield his three inches to move heaven and earth; try to speak a single phrase on the spot.
The Master said, "When meeting a swordsman on the road, one must present a sword; if you are not a poet, do not offer a poem. Lin then ceased.
(See *Wudeng Huiyuan* and *Bingzhi Yue Lu*).
The *Luo Shen Xiang Fei* chapter of the *Chuci* (Songs of Chu) states: "I bid Fenglong ride upon the clouds / To seek out the dwelling place of Fu Fei. The Collected Annotations state:
"Fenglong is the Master of Thunder. Fu Fei was the daughter of Fuxi; she drowned in the Luo River and died, subsequently becoming a river deity."
The table of contents for the "Nine Songs" (*Jiǔgē*) of the *Chuci* lists "Lord Xiang" (*Xiāngjūn*) and "Lady Xiang" (*Xiāngfúren*). The Collected Commentaries state:
Lord Xiang was the eldest daughter of Yao, Ehuang, who became the principal consort of Shun; Lady Xiang was the younger daughter of Yao, Nüying, who was the secondary consort of Shun.

When Shun ascended to the north (died on his journey), he passed away at Cangwu, and the two consorts died between the Yangtze and Xiang rivers. The common people refer to them as the Lord Xiang and others.

Beside the Xiang River there is a temple at Huangling where sacrifices are regularly offered. Hanzi (Han Yu) considered that because Nüwa was the legitimate consort, she was titled "Jun" (Ruler/Lord), whereas Nüying should properly have been addressed as "Furen" (Lady).
Mencius said: "Those who subdue others by force do not win their hearts' submission; it is because their power is insufficient.

Those who subdue others through virtue win the sincere submission of their hearts, for they are pleased in their innermost being. The commentary states: "This refers to those who subdue people by using force while feigning benevolence."
Though they may outwardly comply, they do not truly love or revere him from the heart; they submit merely because their strength is insufficient and have no choice but to yield.
As for one who wins people’s submission through virtue, this is not a forced compliance;
rather, it arises from a heart filled with joy and the utmost sincerity, without any compulsion. This is seen in the "Gongsun Chou" chapter.

"The old drunkard's intent does not lie in the wine," as stated in Ouyang Xiu’s *Record of the Drunken Old Man’s Pavilion*. "All around Chuzhou are mountains. Among the peaks to the southwest, the forests and valleys are particularly beautiful.
Looking at them, they appear lush, deep, and elegant; this is Langye. After traveling six or seven li through the mountains, one gradually begins to hear..."
The sound of water murmuring as it flows between two peaks is that of Nangquan (Wine-Brewing Spring).
Where the peaks wind back and turn, there stands a pavilion, soaring like wings, overlooking the spring: this is Zuiweng Ting (The Pavilion of the Drunken Old Man).
Who built the pavilion? The mountain monk Zhixian. Who gave it its name? The Prefectural Governor himself. It was here that the Governor and his guests came to drink.
I would become intoxicated after drinking only a small amount, and as I was also the oldest among them, I styled myself the "Intoxicated Elder" (Zuìwēng).

The intention of the Intoxicated Elder does not lie in the wine, but rather in the midst of the mountains and waters. The joy of the mountains and waters is perceived by the heart and expressed through wine. (Seen in the *Songwen*).
○ Scroll Five:
The Two Phrases on Exhalation Not Entering into External Conditions.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, while on his way to a meal invitation by the King of East India, [the King]... [text continues].
Question: "Everyone else is reciting the sutras; why do you alone not recite them? The Patriarch said:
"I, this poor monk, do not follow external conditions with my exhalation, nor do I dwell within the aggregates or realms with my inhalation.
I constantly recite such a sutra—hundreds of thousands of ten-thousand million volumes, not merely one or two. (See *Zongmen Tongyao* and *Chanzong Zhengmai*.)

The power of rectifying disorder is found in the *I Ching*: "To rectify the disorders of one's father; having such a son brings no blame to the deceased father. Though there is peril, in the end there is good fortune. The *Xiang* (Image) says:

"To rectify the disorders of one's father means that the intention is to carry on for the deceased father. The commentary states: "Rectifying (*gan*) is like the trunk of a tree—that upon which the branches and leaves depend for their establishment."
"Gǔ" (Worm/Infection) refers to the remnants of what previous persons have already ruined; thus, all the lines contain the image of parents.
If the son can manage them, he will rectify and restore them.
The *Quan yu* chapter of the "Qin Feng" (Airs of Qin) in the *Shijing* states: "For me, there was a great hall, vast and spacious; now, at every meal, there is nothing left over.
Alas! I do not inherit that former abundance. This is an exposition (*fu*). "Great hall" (*xia wu*) refers to a large residence; "vast and spacious" (*qu qu*) describes its depth and breadth.

"Continuity" (*chengji*) means succession; "the beginning" (*quan-yu*) means the commencement. The creation of the balance begins with the weights (*quan*); the creation of the carriage begins with the platform (*yu*).

Therefore, *quan-yu* is called the beginning. It is said that Duke Kang’s reception of the worthy was such that the spirit of ritual propriety gradually declined, and he was unable to continue his initial excellence.
When the Buddha ascended to Tuṣita Heaven, the venomous dragon created obstacles. Maudgalyāyana manifested various forms, both large and small;
Nanda and Upananda, the two dragon brothers, dwelt on the slopes of Mount Sumeru.

Whenever the Buddha would fly through the air up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, the dragon would become resentful and spit forth black clouds and dark mists to obscure the three luminaries, using its body...
It coiled around Mount Sumeru seven times, its tail trailing in the ocean waters and its head resting upon the mountain peak.

Maudgalyāyana then manifested his body twofold, circling Mount Sumeru fourteen times, his tail trailing beyond the outer seas and his head resting upon the Brahma palace. The dragon remained exceedingly wrathful and rained down vajra-grit.
Maudgalyāyana transformed the grit into real flowers, light, soft, and lovely. Still, the dragon’s anger did not cease; thereupon, Maudgalyāyana...
He transformed himself into a minute body and entered within the dragon’s body; he entered through its eyes and emerged from its ears, then entered through its ears and emerged from its nose.
The dragon suffered such agony that its mind was finally subdued, and it beheld Maitreya expounding the meaning of the Dharma.
The non-Buddhist practitioners attempted to move the mountain, but it remained immovable; Maudgalyāyana leveled it into the great earth.
The master and his five hundred disciples of the non-Buddhists used incantations to shift the mountain for an entire month until its base finally began to move.

Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "If this mountain moves, much harm will be done. He immediately sat in the full lotus posture upon the summit of the mountain, and the mountain returned to its original place.
It remained unmoved. The non-Buddhists said to one another, "Our doctrine moves the mountain; we calculated that it would surely shift by now.

Why is it so stable and firm, remaining exactly as it was at first? This must be the work of the śramaṇa. Realizing thus their own weakness, they turned their hearts toward the Buddha-dharma and saw the *Chao-yan-ding-ben*.
Regarding the ancient practice of self-immolation at a deva-temple: Formerly, there was a king of a foreign land who had a daughter named Śunāmukhī. There was also a fisherman named Śūbhaka.
While traveling, he saw the princess from afar within a window on a high tower; he became infatuated with her, and his mind could not let go of her for even a moment. Thus it continued.
Many months passed, yet he was unable to eat or drink. When his mother asked him the reason, he answered her with the truth:
"I saw the king’s daughter and my heart cannot forget her. His mother said, "You are but a man of low station, while the king’s daughter is noble and exalted;

she cannot be obtained. The son replied, "My heart yearns for her and cannot forget her for even a moment. If my wish is not fulfilled, I shall not be able to live. For the sake of her son, the mother entered [the palace].
Within the royal palace, he constantly sent fat fish as gifts to the princess, yet he would not accept payment. The princess, finding this strange, asked him, "What is it that you seek?
Her mother said to the princess, "Please dismiss those around us; I shall tell you the truth.
I have but one son who admires the princess with such devotion that his feelings have become a sickness. His life will not last much longer; I pray you take pity on him and grant him his life."
The King’s daughter said, "Tell her that on the fifteenth day of the month, she should stay behind the image of the deity in a certain shrine.
Her mother returned and told her daughter, "Your wish has been granted. She informed her as instructed; having bathed and put on new clothes, she stayed behind the image of the deity.
When the time arrived, the princess went to her father the King and said, "I have met with an inauspicious omen; I must go to the shrine to seek auspiciousness."
“Excellent,” the king said. He immediately prepared five hundred chariots and proceeded to the temple.
Upon arrival, he commanded his attendants to stop at the gate and entered the temple alone. The deity reflected, “This is not right; the king is my patron.”
"Let us not allow this petty man to bring disgrace upon the princess. He immediately cast a spell upon him, causing him to fall into a deep sleep from which he could not wake.

Once the princess had entered, she saw that he was in a heavy slumber; though she pushed him, he did not awaken. She then left behind for him a necklace worth one hundred thousand taels of gold and departed.
After she had gone, the man woke up and, seeing the necklace, questioned the others, learning that it was the princess who had been there.
He came; his desires unfulfilled, he was filled with grief, resentment, and anguish. The fire of lust flared up within him, burning him to death. (Cited from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*).
The Sixth Patriarch craned his neck [in anticipation].

The monk Zhiche, originally named Xingchang, was surnamed Zhang. In his youth, he was a man of chivalrous spirit. Since the division between the Northern and Southern schools, although the two patriarchs had forgotten self and other, their disciples vied with one another in affection and hatred.
Once this school established Master Xiu as the Sixth Patriarch, [Xingchang] became envious that the robe would be transmitted to him, as this was what was heard throughout the world.
He instructed Xingchang to assassinate the Patriarch; however, the Patriarch’s mind was penetrating and he anticipated this in advance.
He placed ten taels of gold between the seats. Chang entered the room brandishing a blade; the Patriarch extended his neck toward him.
Chang struck three times with the blade, yet it caused no injury at all. The Patriarch said, "A true sword is not crooked; a crooked sword is not true.

I owe you only the gold, but I do not owe you your life. Chang fell down in shock and only regained consciousness after a long time. He begged for mercy and repented, wishing to leave the household life. The Patriarch [granted his request].
He gave him gold and said, "Go for now; I fear the assembly might harm you. Return another day in a different form, and I shall receive you.
Chang received these instructions and fled that night. This is recorded in the *Record of Pointing at the Moon*.
"Like kinds seek one another; like sounds respond to one another," says the *Zhou Yi*.
The Master said: "Like sounds respond to one another; like kinds seek one another. Water flows toward moisture; fire moves toward dryness. Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger.
When the Sage arises, all things behold him. That which is rooted in Heaven is close to what is above; that which is rooted in Earth..."
Those who are similar descend together; thus each follows its own kind. The commentary states: "Wherever sounds are identical, this one will surely sing and that one will respond in harmony.
Wherever natures are identical, this one will surely bestow and that one will receive, seeking one another."

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has established himself in the characteristics of wisdom, he should diligently cultivate and study the three characteristics of supreme noble gnosis (*āryajñāna*).
What are these three characteristics of noble gnosis that should be diligently cultivated?"
Study refers to what is called the mark of non-existence, the mark of the sphere of the self-vow of all Buddhas, and the ultimate mark of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
By practicing, one attains this; having done so, one is able to abandon the mark of the wisdom of the lame donkey mind and attain the eighth stage of the Most Excellent Son (*varaputra*).
The commentary states: "By practicing, one attains this" means that those of sharp faculties in the Shared Teaching contemplate both emptiness and non-emptiness.

One should know that these three aspects are inherently present within a single mind. "The ability to abandon the wisdom of the lame donkey" refers to transcending the wisdom of emptiness possessed by the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*).
The wisdom of the two vehicles, which takes the essence of phenomena as empty, functions only within emptiness and cannot simultaneously function within both emptiness and existence;
therefore, it is called "lame. This is seen in the *Lengqie yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Laṅkāvatāra).
○ Scroll Six: "The False Appropriation of the Divine Vessel" by Luo Binwang.
In the *Proclamation for Xu Jingye’s Campaign against Wu Zetian*, it says: "She has trodden upon the Empress Yuan like a pheasant-feathered robe, plunging us into [misfortune]..."

You have committed incest with your brother’s wives; furthermore, you harbor the hearts of vipers and lizards and possess the nature of jackals and wolves. You have drawn close to the depraved and the perverse, inflicting harm upon the loyal and the good.
You murdered your sister, slaughtered your elder brother, usurped your sovereign, and poisoned your mother. You are loathed by both spirits and men, and neither Heaven nor Earth can tolerate you.
Yet you still conceal your malevolent intent and covet the sacred regalia of state. (As seen in the *Tang Wen*.)
"Extensive charity and saving the multitude.
Zi Gong said, "If there were one who practiced extensive charity upon the people and was able to save the multitude, how would he be? Could he be called benevolent?
The Master said, "What need is there even to speak of benevolence? He must be a sage. Even Yao and Shun found it difficult to achieve this. The commentary states: "Benevolence is the mind..."
The goal is infinite, yet the capacity for measurement is limited. To bestow benefits extensively and rescue the multitude—how could this be achieved by benevolence (*ren*) alone?
It must be the sage who embodies the Way of Benevolence in its entirety and reaches its ultimate limit who can accomplish it.
Yet even sages such as Yao and Shun felt a sense of deficiency in their hearts, as if they were always lacking something; this is seen in the *Analects*, Part One.

"Love one's kin and extend benevolence to the people. Mencius said: "The gentleman loves all things but does not treat them with benevolence; he treats the people with benevolence but does not treat them as his own kin.

He loves his kin and extends benevolence to the people; he extends benevolence to the people and loves all things. The commentary states: "The gentleman gives priority to the single root [of human relationships]."

One uses kindness to treat one's own kin as dear; yet, by extending the thought of cherishing one's kin to love the people, one cannot simply apply to the people the same treatment reserved for one's kin.
One expands the measure of regarding all people as brothers to love the people;

yet, by extending the heart that loves the people to care for all things, one cannot simply apply to all things the same treatment reserved for the people. This is what is meant by "exhausting [the capacity of] seeing."
Chapter on the Mind.

Regarding the "Three Dignitaries" (Santai), Zhu Xi’s *Commentary on the Elementary Learning* (*Xiaoxue Jizhu*) states: "In the Zhou dynasty, the Grand Preceptor (Taishi), Grand Tutor (Taifu), and Grand Guardian (Taobao) constituted the Three Ducal Ministers (Sanguogong). In the Eastern Han..."

The Grand Marshal (Taishǒu), the Minister of Education (Sìtóng), and the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) constitute the Three Dukes (Sāngōng). The *Tiānwén Zhì* (Annals of Astronomy) states: "The Three Terraces (Sāntái) consist of six stars, arranged in pairs.
The two stars nearest to Wénchāng on the west are called the Upper Terrace; the next two stars are called the Middle Terrace; and the two stars to the east are called the Lower Terrace.
In relation to humanity, they represent the positions of the Three Dukes. The *Zhèngzì Tōng* states: "The name of the Three Terrace stars; also referred to as 'the Terrace Cauldrons' (Táidǐng)."

The title of the "Three Dukes" (Sāngōng) is like the stars having the Three Terraces (Sāntái) or a tripod having three legs. Furthermore, in the second year of King Wu of Qin, the position of Chancellor (Chánhxiàng) was first established.
Moreover, the "Four Supports" (Sìfǔ)—the Advisor (Fù), the Assistant (Bǐ), the Consultant (Yí), and the Vice-Chancellor (Chéng)—are so called. One who assists me by standing beside me is called a Fù;
one who assists me by brushing away errors is called a Bǐ; one who stands before me to deliberate is called a Yí; and one who follows behind me to support my actions is called a Chéng. Furthermore...
The names of the four auxiliary stars: these four stars assist the North Pole.
Regarding the "three obediences" (*sān cóng*), Confucius said, "A woman is one who submits to others. Therefore, she possesses no principle of independent authority; she has three obediences.

The Way of women is this: while at home they follow their fathers; when married, they follow their husbands; and when their husbands die, they follow their sons. They dare not act according to their own will.
This passage is from Zhu Xi’s *Elementary Learning* (*Xiǎoxué*), and it is largely identical with slight variations to the *Book of Rites* and the *Family Sayings* (*Jiāyǔ*).

As for the four virtues: first is the virtue of a wife, which consists of integrity and docility; second is the speech of a wife, which consists of courtesy and command; third is the appearance of a wife, which consists of gentleness and amiability; fourth is the work of a wife, which consists of silk and... [woolen].

Master Fenggan originally resided at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. One day, while out for a stroll, he encountered Lü Qiu Yin, who was departing for his post as the Governor of Taizhou.
Just as he was about to set out for the capital, he suddenly suffered from a severe headache; though he summoned renowned physicians, none could cure him. It happened that Fenggan arrived there.
He sprinkled it with pure water, and in an instant, [the pestilence] was entirely dispelled. Consequently, he developed great reverence and asked where they had come from.
They replied, "From Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. He asked, "Are there any sages there? They said, "Hanshan is Mañjuśrī and Shide is Samantabhadra;
you should go there to see them. Three days after Qiu Yin took up his post, he went to the temple and asked, "Has this temple ever had the Chan master Fenggan?"
The Master said, "Is that so? At that time, the monk Daoqiao replied, "It is. The Master asked, "Where is the monastery located? And who are Hanshan and Shide?
Daoqiao replied, "Fenggan’s old monastery is behind the sutra repository; it is currently said to be unoccupied, with only tigers and leopards coming there to roar.
The two, Hanshan and Shide, are currently serving as laborers in the monastic kitchen. Qiu Yin entered Fenggan’s [monastery].
In the room, he saw only tiger tracks crisscrossing about. He asked Gan, "What kind of practice have you been engaged in while here?

Gan replied, "I have only been occupied with husking grain to provide rice gruel for the monks. After he had sighed in admiration three times over this, he entered the kitchen and saw two people bowing to him.
The two men rose and ran away, saying, "Fenggan is too talkative! You do not even recognize Amitābha; why do you prostrate yourself before us? Then they took each other's hands and departed.
At the Pine Gate, he no longer entered the monastery. This is detailed in the *Biographies of Divine Monks* (*Shenseng zhuan*).
Regarding Du Shun, the First Patriarch of the Dharma-realm School: Master Du Shun was named Fashun; his imperial title was Dixin. His secular surname was Du.
He was a native of Duling in Wannian County, Yongzhou. He was born in the second year of the Yongding era of Emperor Wu of the Chen dynasty.

At the age of fifteen, he took his brother’s place on a military expedition; he did not raise a blade, and the enemy forces immediately retreated. Having no desire for official honor, he requested to return home to care for his parents.

Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty summoned him and said, "I am suffering from a fever that has not been cured for a long time. By what means can your divine power dispel it?
The Master replied, "Your Majesty’s sagely virtue governs the realm; how could demonic forces prevail? Simply issue a general amnesty, and Your Majesty’s health will surely be restored."
The Emperor accepted the Master’s words and issued a general amnesty for the empire. The Emperor’s illness was subsequently cured. He was granted the title "Heart of the Emperor.
In the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, the Master passed away while seated at Yishan Temple in the Southern Suburb. He was eighty-four years of age. Before his passing, the Master...

He went to look for Amitābha, but the monk did not understand his meaning and departed. Upon reaching Mount Tai, he encountered an elderly gentleman who asked, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "I have come to pay homage to Mañjuśrī. The gentleman said, "Mañjuśrī is not on this mountain at present; what benefit is there in your coming? The monk said:
“Where is Mañjuśrī now? The gentleman replied, “He has gone to Chang’an to teach and transform sentient beings.
The monk said, “I am a native of Chang’an; who currently acts as Mañjuśrī there? The gentleman replied, “The Venerable Dushun is Mañjuśrī himself.
Upon hearing this, the monk stood up straight and cried out in astonishment, “Dushun is my teacher! Suddenly, the old gentleman vanished.

it took three full days for them to cross. When they arrived at the monastery, the Master had already passed away the previous day. It was only then that he understood this to have been an emanation of Mañjuśrī.

○ Volume Seven, *The Ritual Standards of the Vinaya on the Unmanifest Precept-Substance* states:
At the time of receiving the precepts, one generates a mind of the highest grade (*uttama-karman*) and exerts the power of mental action (*cetanā-karman*). It proceeds...

One contemplates the *dharmadhātu*. Taking as its object all sentient and insentient things, there arises upon those objects an unconditioned form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) consisting of non-lust, non-killing, non-stealing, non-lying, and so forth. This form is not composed of the four great elements;

therefore, it is called "unconditioned" (*avijñapti*). Nor is it blue, yellow, red, white, or the like; therefore, it is called "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*). Once this has arisen, it constantly relies upon—
In the mind, one maintains constant mindfulness and guards it at all times. Thus, form is that which relies [upon something], while the mind is that upon which it relies;
the mind is that which protects, while form is that which is protected. The union of mind and form is called the essence of the precepts (*śīla*).
Regarding the four virtues of Qian, the *Xiangci* (Image Commentary) of the *Qian* hexagram in the *Zhouyi* states: "Qian: Yuan, Heng, Li, and Zhen. The *Wenyan* (Text on the Words) says:
"Yuan is the eldest of the good; Heng is the gathering of the auspicious; Li is the harmony of righteousness; and Zhen is the backbone of affairs. The Ruler...

The Son of Heaven embodies benevolence (*ren*), which is sufficient to lead others. His auspicious assemblies are sufficient to accord with ritual propriety (*li*). His benefiting of things is sufficient to harmonize with righteousness (*yi*).

His steadfastness and solidity are sufficient to serve as the backbone for affairs. Because the noble person practices these four virtues, it is said: "Qian is Great Primordiality; success, advantage, and perseverance. The commentary states:
"Great Primordiality" (*yuan*) is the initial manifestation of the virtue of Qian. It provides the beginning for the myriad things, such that each thing obtains its own life-giving benevolence.

Therefore, it is the preeminent excellence of goodness. "Penetration" (*heng*) refers to the unimpeded flow of things as they grow; it is the stream of formative growth that brings forth transformation.
It wields the moisture of moving clouds and falling rain, and thus constitutes the assembly of excellence.

"Advantage" (*li*) means that the Way of Qian does not act alone, but joins its virtue with that of Kun to accomplish the work of benefiting all things; thus, it is the harmony of righteousness. "Constancy" (*zhen*) means to preserve and harmonize.

Great Harmony (Tàihé) is the coalescence of integrity and solidity; it is the source from which the life-force and nature of the myriad things exist and from which their ceaseless benevolence (*rén*) is renewed and manifested.

Therefore, it constitutes the backbone of all affairs. When the noble person (*jūnzǐ*) emulates the primacy of Great Beginning (*yuán*), they are able to embody the source of benevolence and love others;
thus, they are sufficient to lead others. By practicing the prosperity of auspicious gathering (*jiāhuì*), they are able to bring together beauty and excellence through ritual propriety (*lǐ*).
Thus, it is sufficient to accord with ritual (*li*). By means of this appropriate benefit, one assists the multitude; thus, it is sufficient to harmonize with righteousness (*yi*).
By means of this steadfast and firm maintenance, one serves as the central ruler; thus, it is sufficient to manage affairs.

When a gentleman practices these four virtues—meaning that a gentleman is able to practice the four virtues of benevolence (*ren*), righteousness (*yi*), ritual (*li*), and wisdom (*zhi*)—he accords with *yuan*, *hen*, *li*, and *zhen*.
This is the Way of Heaven; thus, human nature and heavenly nature merge into one. Regarding the *Gengluo* and *Mingling*, the *Shijing* says:
"The *mingling* has offspring; the *gengluo* carries them. The commentary states: "The *mingling* is a small green insect upon the mulberry tree."
The *si bu qu* is the *guo luo*, the earth wasp. It resembles a bee but has a slender waist; it captures silkworm larvae and carries them into a hollow in a tree.
It chants: "Be like me! Be like me! After seven days, they transform into its offspring. This is from the "Xiaowan" chapter of the *Xiaoya* in the *Shijing*.

Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the “Preface to the Separate Commentary on the Chapter on Vows and Practices” states: “The dharma-gate of a single word cannot be fully recorded even with the ink of the ocean;

Within one gate; within one gate, one dharma; within one dharma, one meaning; within one meaning, one phrase—even so little as a single part cannot be found.
How much less could one possibly write it down in its entirety? The commentary states: "Even so little as a single part" refers to a single character.
Because the single character that expresses [the meaning] is itself entirely identical to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) that is expressed, it is therefore inexhaustible.
Unlike other schools, that which expresses is certainly not the same as that which is expressed. The *Commentary on Yongming’s Heart-Essence赋* states:
"Even if one were to gather Mount Sumeru to serve as a brush, it would still fail to write down a single sentence or a single verse of the *Puyan Jing* (Universal Eye Sutra)."

The *Guǎngzhì* on Hain-juice states: The hain-poisonous bird is as large as a hawk. Its neck is eight inches long, its feathers are purple-green, and its entire body is poisonous.

When it ascends into the air, the sun and moon lose their luster; when it lands, the vegetation within one hundred *li* in each of the four directions all withers.
It crouches or lies upon mountain rocks as high and broad as Mount Sumeru, yet it can be shattered like dust. Its excrement falls from a height of ten thousand *yojana*.
Upon striking these stones, it passes through to the bottom as if shot by an arrow. Those who see it go blind and break out in sores; those who catch its reflection lose consciousness.
How much more so for its feathers or dung! Furthermore, a verse says: "Meeting this bird is like encountering the three evil poisons;
wherever it goes, the grass withers. Its feathers soaked in wine produce flames; once inside the belly, they dye it three parts blue. (Seen in the *Baoxun*).
Regarding the category of pearls:
they were square and long, yet did not break.
Song Cheng Yi, courtesy name Zhengshu, a native of Luoyang, served as the Lecturer for the Chongzheng Hall. At that time, Emperor Zhezong playfully broke one.
Liu Zhi submitted a memorial, advising: "As it is the springtime of growth and flourishing, one must not wantonly break off branches without cause. The Emperor accepted this advice;
having perceived the meaning of the *Fayin* (Revealing the Hidden), he did not clear away the weeds in his courtyard.
Zhou Dunyi of the Song dynasty, courtesy name Maoshu, was a native of Chongling. One day, upon meeting Foyin, he attained a realization. He would not clear away the weeds growing by his window;
when people asked him why, he replied, "They share the same essence as my own mind. Thus, he composed the lines: "The weeds grow deep outside the window, making one never tired of looking at them.
This is recorded in the *Dacheng yinyi* (Meaning and Phonetics of the Mahāyāna).
"I wish to diminish my transgressions but have not yet succeeded.
Qu Boyu sent an envoy to Confucius. Confucius had him sit down and questioned him, saying, "What is your master doing?
He replied, "My master wishes to diminish his transgressions but has not yet succeeded. After the envoy had left, the Master said, "A true messenger indeed!"
"An envoy. The commentary states: "He was made to sit; this was out of respect for his master, which extended to his envoy as well. The Master [Confucius] was referring to Bo Yu.

To say that he merely wished to diminish his transgressions yet had not yet succeeded reveals the sense that his self-examination and self-mastery were always as if he were falling short. See the *Analects*, Part II.

Regarding the two lines, "Its wisdom is all-encompassing like a mirror yet eternally still," the *Preface to the Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "As for its fundamental purport: it darkly unifies with the true essence within the realm of myriad transformations; it manifests the marks of virtue at the gate of the 'twofold mystery.
Its function arises profusely yet remains eternally as-it-is; its wisdom is all-encompassing like a mirror yet eternally still. Thus, its function is manifold while its wisdom is...

"Permeating" (zhou) means that while wondrous functions arise in profusion, they do not depart from the true essence of suchness; while numinous wisdom universally reflects, it remains eternally in the state of quiescent extinction.
It is like a narrow path through the mountains: through the repeated treading of it, it becomes a road.
Mencius said to Gaozi: "The principles of propriety and righteousness within the human heart are fundamentally free from obstruction.
Nevertheless, one must examine and reflect upon them at all times; they must not be interrupted for even a single breath. Have you not observed the footpaths on mountain trails?

A mountain trail is merely a place where a person's tracks can be seen; it is not originally a great highway. Yet, if people were to pass back and forth through it in rapid succession, it would eventually become [a major road]."

Regarding the great highway that has been leveled and smoothed: once it is completed, after a short while, when human tracks become rare, it is again blocked by weeds and brush. See the commentary on the text.

Master Yongjia, whose numinous spirit was hidden within the *dharmadhātu*, replied in a letter to his friend, Chan Master Lang of Mount Zu Xi: "Wandering at ease through the mountains and valleys, roaming freely amidst the outskirts and market towns;
my physical form is relaxed and leisurely, while my inner heart is tranquil and still. Serenity rests within, and a detached composure radiates outward."

Externally, his body appeared as if constrained; internally, his mind was as if expansive. He manifested his physical form throughout the universe while his profound spirit remained hidden within the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus, he responded to conditions through resonance, acting spontaneously without fixed standard. See the *Benji* (Collection of Fundamentals).
The *Appended Statements* of the *Zhouyi* say: "It encompasses the transformations of Heaven and Earth without excess; it brings all things to completion in their particularity without omission;
it penetrates the way of day and night and thus possesses knowledge. Therefore, the Spirit has no fixed location, and the *Yi* has no fixed form. The commentary states: "This..."
The Sage understands the matter of destiny. "Pattern" (*fan*) refers to having a mold or model, like casting metal; "encompassing" (*wei*) refers to the surrounding boundaries.

The transformations of Heaven and Earth are inexhaustible, yet the Sage establishes their pattern and boundaries so as not to allow them to exceed the Middle Way—this is what is meant by "shaping and completing.
"Pervasive" (*tong*) means comprehensive. Day and night refer to the dark and the bright, life and death, and ghosts and spirits. As it says:
Only after this can one perceive the subtlety of the Supreme Spirit. It has no fixed location; the transformations of the *I Ching* have no physical form.
When you hold a handle against a handle to shape wood, the principle is not far from you.
The Odes say: "To hew the handle, to hew the handle, its model is not far off. One grasps the handle to hew the handle; yet looking askance at it, one still deems it distant.

Therefore, the gentleman governs men by means of men, ceasing once they have reformed. The Commentary says: This is from the "Hewing the Handle" (*Fako*) chapter of the *Odes* of the *Youfeng* (Mystic Airs).
"Handle" (*ke*) refers to the handle of an axe; "model" (*ze*) refers to the standard. "Looking askance" (*ni*) means looking obliquely. It means that when a person grasps a handle to hew wood...

As for the branch: the principles of length and shortness regarding that branch reside in this very branch. Yet, there still exists a distinction between "this" and "that," so when the woodcutter looks at it, he still perceives it as distant.
If one governs people by means of people, then the Way of being human resides within the body of each person concerned;
from the outset, there is no distinction between "this" and "that. Therefore, when a gentleman governs people, [he does so in this manner].
"Apply to that person the very way they have used against others; if that person can reform, then stop and do not punish them.
This means one holds them accountable for what they are capable of knowing and practicing, rather than desiring them to distance themselves from humanity in order to constitute the Way.
See the *Zhongyong*.
"Carrying Mount Hua and Mount Yue, shaking the Yellow River and the sea, neither heavy nor leaking"—so it is said in the *Zhongyong*.

Now, as for the earth: though it may be no more than a handful of soil, in its vastness and thickness, it carries Mount Hua and Mount Yue without feeling heavy, and shakes the Yellow River and the sea without leaking;
all things rest upon it. The commentary states: "Now, as for the earth" refers to a single location.

Even a handful of soil is earth. Were one to discuss its vastness and thickness, Mount Hua and Mount Yue could support it without it becoming heavy, and the rivers and seas could contain it without it being lost.
Thus, among all the myriad disparate things, there is nothing that does not exist within its sustaining and supporting.

The poem "Huang Liu" (Yellow Flow) says: "Dense is that jade libation cup; the yellow flow is within it. The term "yu" (with) indicates this. "Sè" (dense) describes the appearance of being fine and compact. The "yù zàn" (jade libation cup) is the "guī zàn" (jade-handled libation cup).
It has a jade handle, a ladle made of gold, an exterior of blue metal, and its interior is vermilion. The "huáng liú" (yellow flow) refers to the sacrificial wine.
It refers to the *yùchàng* (fragrant wine). One brews *jùshǔ* millet into wine, then builds up *yùjīn* (turmeric) and boils it to blend with the liquor, so that its fragrance is rich and pervasive.
It is poured from a *zàn* ladle for the libation. This describes how the fine and dense jade *zàn* is a precious vessel of the ancestral temple;

thus, what is contained within must be the "yellow flow" (*huángliú*). "Yellow" signifies that its color is correct, and "flowing" signifies that its fragrance extends far. [From] the *Dà...* (The Great...).
Regarding the "Decade on King Ya Wen":

the *Ganlu Zongjing* (Mirror of the Ambrosial Essence) states that there is a tree of ambrosia. During the mid-autumn month, dew drips onto its leaves; those who take it use it as an elixir for longevity.
If one enters the stages [of the bodhisattva path], they transform into a jewel; this is like the Dharma entering the mind upon hearing it, transforming into the seed of Bodhi.

Regarding the saying "to glue the pegs while playing the se," which means using the laws of past sages to govern the future—this is like gluing the pegs of a lute to tune it—is there such a thing? It is said: [Yes].
There is such a thing. It is said: "Sage rulers are few while mediocre rulers are many; this is like adhering solely to the Way of Zhongni. It is further said:
"The laws of the sages have never failed to be concerned with the rise and fall [of dynasties]. This is from the "Chapter on Foreknowledge" (*Zhiqian*) in Yangzi’s *Fayen*.
Regarding the statement in the *Preface to the Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

"The wisdom of the Eastern Temple’s Enlightenment is no different from the initial resolve," the phrase "the Eastern Temple’s Enlightenment" refers to the sixty-second fascicle of the Sūtra, which says: "At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva exhorted the bhikṣus..."

Having generated the bodhicitta, he gradually traveled south until he reached the eastern side of the City of Blessings (Puṇyavatī), where he stayed in the Śāla Forest of the Adorned Banner (*Vyūhadhvaja*) at the site of a great stūpa where Buddhas of the past had taught and transformed sentient beings. The commentary states: "This is the Eastern Temple.
At that time, the people of the City of Blessings heard that the Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta was at the great stūpa within the Śāla Forest of the Adorned Banner.
At that temple site, an immeasurable multitude emerged from the city and came to where he was. Among them were five hundred youths, and Sudhana was one of them.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī specifically observed Sudhana, comforted and instructed him, and expounded all the Buddha-dharmas for him, until he caused him to rejoice and resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhicitta. Furthermore, he causes them to recollect their past roots of goodness, and then departs to preach the Dharma to sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, having heard these various merits of the Buddha from Mañjuśrī, single-mindedly and diligently sought Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is the awakening of the light of wisdom. Wisdom.
This is no different from the case of a beginner. As the Eightieth Sūtra states:
"At that time, Mañjuśrī extended his right hand from afar, across a distance of one hundred and ten yojanas, and placed it upon the crown of Sudhana’s head, saying:

'Excellent, excellent, son of good family! If you are devoid of the root of faith, if your mind is weak, regretful, and filled with anxiety, and if your meritorious practices are incomplete, you will fall away and lose your diligence.'"
They are diligent, yet their minds become attached to a single root of virtue; they consider a small amount of merit to be sufficient;

they are unable to skillfully initiate practices and vows; and they are unable to fully comprehend such a nature of phenomena, such a principle, such a dharma-gate, such a mode of conduct and abiding, or such a sphere of experience—whether it be to know them universally, or to exhaust their very source. Or...

"Understood. Even if one were to attain it, [the following] would all be impossible. The commentary states: "To thoroughly understand the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and below constitutes the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pūrṇa*).
If one is separated from faith (*śraddhā*), then one cannot attain it; conversely, this reveals that by means of faith, one attains it without departing from the initial mind.
Thus, faith and wisdom are non-dual (*advaya*). If one says that immovable wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*) is the beginning, then the two wisdoms—prior and subsequent—are non-dual. This is the vision.
In the *Huayan Xuantan* (Profound Discourse on the Avataṃsaka),
it quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "When the sun first rises, one sees city gates, watchtowers, and palaces, with people coming and going."
As the sun rises higher, it gradually vanishes; it can only be seen with the eyes and possesses no reality. This is called a *gandharvanagara* (city of the gandharvas).
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "The 'dry city' is colloquially called 'sea-mist. The *shen* is a large clam. It arises over sea-islands at dawn; when viewed from afar, it appears to exist."

Upon close inspection, they are non-existent. The Venerable Daozhen’s *Praise Using the Simile of the Gandharva City* says: "The phenomena of the world are empty and vast, like that city of the gandharvas;
at dawn, shadows spread, and this capital city appears. The foolish rush toward it, marching along with the wind;
only at day's end do they realize their error, wailing in distress as they lose their voices. I saw this in the *Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Regarding the initial step as the journey of a thousand li, the *Zhao lun* states:
"The long road relies upon the initial step. The commentary cites the Master of Lao [Laozi]: "A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet.
"Relying upon" means that by depending on the initial step, one is able to reach the thousand li; the intent is to use the thousand li as a metaphor.

The fruit. The initial step serves as a metaphor for the cause. From the first step to the thousandth, and from the thousandth li back to the first step, the original step does not change. Through practice one realizes the fruit;
when the path to the fruit is perfected, the original cause remains eternally manifest.
"A single basketful initiates a mountain ten thousand *chi* high. The *Zhao lun* says:
"The completion of a mountain depends upon the accumulation of the first basketful. The commentary cites the *Analects*: "It is like building a mountain;

even if one has covered but a single basketful, if one proceeds, one is moving forward. A *kui* (basketful) is a basket of earth. "Depends upon" (*jia jiu*) means that the mountain [is established] by depending upon that very first basketful.

Accomplishment. Here, the mountain is used as a metaphor for the fruit, while the first basket of earth serves as a metaphor for the initial cause. As soil is accumulated to form a mountain, once the mountain is complete, the initial effort becomes even more manifest.
As the cultivation of practice brings about the fruit, once the fruit is perfected, the original cause remains all the more evident.

The "Zhunsheng" chapter of the *Mencius*, "Li Lou," states: "Once the sages had exhausted the power of their eyesight, they followed this with compasses, squares, levels, and plumb lines to ensure squareness, roundness, levelness, and straightness;
these tools were used beyond measure. The commentary notes: "The sages of antiquity desired to fashion vessels..."
To serve the practical needs of the world, he had already exhausted his visual acuity in discerning the standards of squareness, roundness, levelness, and straightness.
However, if there were no means to perpetuate these standards, his visual power would eventually reach its limit.

Therefore, he fashioned the compass and square to produce squareness and roundness, and the level and line to produce levelness and straightness, so that all people of future generations might rely upon them as their standard.
"Shi. This is the method for the sages' creation of vessels; its uses are inexhaustible. Regarding the Seal of State, according to Cai Yong’s *Duduan*:

"The Emperor possesses six seals, all of which are made of jade with a coiled dragon and tiger-claw handle. Their inscriptions read: 'The Emperor’s Seal of Action,' 'The Emperor’s Seal of Command,' [and so forth]."

The Imperial Seal; the Emperor’s Seal of Credence; the Seal for the Son of Heaven’s Dispatches; the Seal of the Son of Heaven; and the Seal of Credence of the Son of Heaven—all of these were sealed with purple clay from the Wu-gong Mountain.
One of these was called the "Seal of Credence" (*xìn*). In antiquity, both the honored and the humble shared its use.

Since the Qin and Han dynasties, however, only the Supreme Sovereign has been entitled to call it a "seal" (*xiǎn*). During the reign of the Lesser Emperor of the Later Han, following the chaos caused by the Ten Eunuchs, this seal was lost. The [Wu]... [dynasty].
Sun Jian was campaigning against Dong Zhuo and was stationed at the site of the abandoned palace in Northern Luoyang.

One night, he observed a radiant light in the southeastern corner and ordered his soldiers to search for its source in a well. Upon dredging the well, they recovered it. He questioned Cheng Pu, who replied, "This is the Imperial Seal of State.
In the past, when the First Emperor of Qin unified the world, he obtained the jade of Bian He and commanded Li Si—"
It was inscribed with eight characters in seal script (*zhuànshū*). The inscription read: "Mandated by Heaven; having received it, may there be eternal prosperity.
From this point on, it became the Seal of the Succession of States (*chuánguó zhǐ*). It was transmitted through two dynasties until Emperor Gao of Han entered Xianyang and obtained it.

It was passed down through twelve emperors. When Wang Mang usurped the throne, the Empress Dowager struck and broke off one corner of it; later, it was repaired with gold. During the reign of Guangwu, the dynasty was restored, and [the seal] was transmitted...

"Up to the present day, that my lord has obtained it is the will of Heaven. (This is recorded in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, following the "Annals of Emperor Gao of Han," where the phrase "the old man of the Lü clan was in hesitation" appears;
"hesitation" [yóuyù] is also the name of two animals, both of which are numerous.)
It is doubtful; therefore, it is used as a metaphor. One explanation states: because it is full of suspicion and doubt, upon hearing the sound of a person, it immediately climbs a tree;

only after a long time, when no one is seen, does it descend. Yet, in an instant, it climbs back up again. This occurs more than once, and thus its hesitation and indecision are called *youyu* (hesitation). See the *Zengbu Zihui* (Supplement to the Dictionary of Characters).
"Please enter the jar," [said Lai Junchen].
During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian of the Tang dynasty, someone reported that Zhou Xing had conspired with Qiu Shennji. Empress Wu ordered Lai Junchen to interrogate him.
While Lai Junchen and Xing were discussing the case over a meal, Lai said to Xing, "Prisoners often do not confess; I shall [act as their advocate]..."
"What law? Xing asked. [The official] replied, "We will place the prisoner in a jar and roast him with fire; what crime would he not then confess?
Li Junchen then requested a large jar and surrounded it with fire according to Xing's instructions. He then rose and said to Xing, "There is an internal memorial impeaching you, your elder brother.

I request that you enter this jar. Terrified, Xing prostrated himself and confessed his crimes. He was subsequently exiled to Lingnan, where he was murdered by his enemies. (From the *Guang hongming ji*).

Regarding the "Nangpu" (Sack) of the two younger brothers in the *Shiji*: the First Emperor "nangpu"ed his two younger brothers because they were born of the illicit union between the Empress Dowager and Lü Du.
When the First Emperor discovered this, he placed them in leather sacks, lifted them up, and smothered them to death. This is also seen in the *Lieguo zhi*.

It is a worldly tradition that the *chāng* ghost rides upon a tiger. When a tiger bites a person and the person dies, their soul dares not go elsewhere; it is instead made to serve the tiger and is named a *chāng* ghost.
When the tiger goes out to seek food, the *chāng* must accompany it and act as its guide. If they encounter a path where there are hidden traps or pits, [the *chāng*] then detours...
He went on his way. He called out to the tiger, saying, "When a general dies, one weeps for him. Li Tanyu’s *Zongtan* says:
"When a person encounters a tiger, their clothes and sash unfasten themselves; they all lay them aside on the ground. Only after the tiger sees the person naked does it eat them.
This is all the doing of the *chāng* (the wandering spirit). The *chāng* may indeed be called the most foolish among ghosts."
In Qi, there was a one-legged bird known as the Shāngyáng that danced upon the water. It flew and alighted upon the public court, spreading its wings and hopping about.

The Marquis of Qi found this strange and dispatched an envoy to Lu to consult Confucius. The Master said, "This bird is named Shāngyáng; it is an omen of rain. Long ago, when children were playing..."
He shook his feet and leaped about, singing a ditty: "The heavens are about to send down a great rain; the *shāngyáng* dances. Now it is here in Qi; its fulfillment is imminent.
Quickly inform the people to hasten the clearing of drains and canals and the repair of embankments; a great flood is coming as a calamity."
Recently there was a great deluge, and the rainwater overflowed its banks, causing damage to the people across various states; only Qi was prepared and thus did not suffer defeat.
Duke Jing said, "The words of the sages are indeed true and bear witness. This is from the "Discerning Governance" chapter of the *Kongzi Jiayu*.
Regarding the *fēiyí* (肥遺), the *Shān-hǎi jīng* (山海經) states:

"On Mount Dàhuá (大華山) there is a serpent named *fēiyí* (phonetic transcription: wèi), which has six feet and four wings; when it appears, a great drought occurs throughout the world. It is also written as *fēiyí*.
In the *Shǔ Táo'ū* (蜀檮杌) by Zhāng Tángyīng of the Sòng dynasty, it says: "During the Qián dé (乾德) era of Shǔ Wáng Yǎn..."
In the third year, there was no rain for five months. By the ninth month, the *feiyi* appeared behind the Red Tower.
Xin Yinxun of Shu, while compiling the *Wangshi Kaiguo Ji*, identified the *feiyi* as the drought-demon *hanba*. According to the records, the *feiyi* is a type of snake with fire upon its horns.
"Seeing it, one realizes that drought is not caused by the *pāpa* (the demoness);
understanding this, one sees that karmic obstructions are originally empty.

These two lines refer to what the Great Master Yongjia said in his *Song of Enlightenment*: "It is also foolishness; it is also petty stupidity. From an empty fist, one produces the notion of a real thing."
[The Master] said: "To grasp at the finger as being the moon is to labor in vain; within the phenomena of sense-faculties and objects, you are falsely fabricating strange delusions.
When you do not see even a single dharma, you may then be called Avalokiteśvara. Once it is realized, karmic obstacles are fundamentally empty; if it is not realized, one must repay past debts.
[He] offered a bright moon [as an offering]. He questioned Master Changsha Cen: "An ancient worthy said, 'Once it is realized, karmic..."
Obstructions are originally empty; if one has not realized this, one must repay past debts.

As for Venerable Siṃha and the Great Master the Second Patriarch, why did they nevertheless go on to repay their debts? Zhaozhou said, "Virtuous One, you do not recognize that they are originally empty.
Yunmen asked, "What is 'originally empty'? Zhaozhou said, "Karmic obstructions are. Yunmen asked, "What are karmic obstructions? Zhaozhou said, "'Originally empty' is."

This was so. Yue remained silent. Sha indicated this to him with a verse, saying: "That which is provisionally existent is fundamentally not existent; that which is provisionally extinguished is likewise not non-existent.
This is the meaning of Nirvana as the settling of debts; its single nature is no different. See the *Record of Pointing at the Moon*.
To rectify one’s thoughts and incline toward Bodhi, only the human path is capable [of this].
In the Preface to the Commentary on the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué shū xù), Master Pí says: "Alas! That by which sentient beings come and go are the six realms."

The ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of deep-seated sorrow; birds and beasts harbor the grief of frantic agitation; the asuras are in the midst of rage; and the devas are immersed in pleasure.
Only those who can rectify their mental deliberations and advance toward Bodhi are capable of this—and that is only the human path. If one is human and yet does not do so, [one is lost].
"I can do nothing for him; it is already too late.
The Imperial Preface to the *Anthology of the Sayings of Chan Masters Through the Ages* states: "In sum, this matter is like the bright sun, like a great..."

Regarding the "mass of fire": if one "presents" it, one presents it in its entirety; if one "seals" it, one seals it in its entirety. Otherwise, one fails to grasp the Buddha’s true intent and belongs entirely to those who merely plunder and toy with the spirit.
The "Ten Immortals" of today, who do not practice according to the True Awakening, are precisely of this sort.
The *Inner Biography of the Lord Maos* (*Maoshan neizhuan*) states: "Mount Mao is also known as Mount Jujue. During the Qin dynasty, it was called the Huayang Cave-Heaven (*dongtian*).
The *Hetu* says: 'The land of Mount Wen is the Well-Lattice (*jingluo*), the assembly site of Heaven where the spirits establish blessings; above it is..."*
The *Tianjing* (Celestial Vault). The *Liezi* states: "To the east of the Bohai Sea there is a great ocean. Within it are mountains:
the first is called Dayu, the second Yuanqiao, the third Fanghu, the fourth Yingzhou, and the fifth Penglai.
Upon them are terraces and pavilions, and trees of gold, jade, pearls, and crystal all growing in dense clusters. Their fruits all possess exquisite flavors; eating them..."
The dead—everyone becomes an immortal sage. Day and night they fly back and forth. Those of the world have meager merit; how could they possibly reach this place?

Regarding Langyuan and Kunlun, the *Hanshu* (Book of Han) contains a note on Mount Kunlun: it is over two thousand five hundred li high, where the sun and moon alternate in concealment and appearance.
Radiant Light. The *Shizhou ji* (Record of the Ten Islands of Bohai) states: "The mountain has three peaks.
One peak points directly toward the North Pole and is named Langfeng Ridge (which is the Immortal Garden). One peak points directly west and is named Xuampu Terrace. One peak points directly east."
It is named the Kunlun Palace, with five walls and twelve towers, all of which are inhabited by immortals.
Chan Master Weiyen of Yaoshan in Lizhou first visited Shitou; as their karmic conditions were not yet aligned, he next paid homage to Mazu.
Understanding his point of return upon hearing these words, he returned once more to Shitou. One day, while sitting on a rock, Shitou asked him, "What are you doing here?
He replied, "I am doing nothing at all. Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are just sitting idly.
He replied, "If it were idle sitting, then I would be doing something. Shitou asked, "You say you do nothing; what is it that you do not do? He replied, "Even the thousand sages..."
He did not recognize him. The Head praised him with a verse, saying: "Living together from the start, we have known each other's names not;

Moving along together as we please, we simply walk thus. Even the sages of antiquity could not know him; How could ordinary people of haste and folly understand him? Later, while residing at Yaoshan, his school of thought flourished greatly.
Li Ao, the Prefect of Langzhou, having heard of the Master’s profound transformation, repeatedly invited him but he did not go. Thereupon, Li Ao went in person to pay his respects.
The Master held his scripture volume and did not look up. The attendant said, "The Governor is here.

Li was of a narrow and impatient temperament, so he remarked, "A face seen is not as good as a name heard," and swept his sleeves, departing at once. The Master said, "How can the Governor hold ears dear while deprecating eyes?"
Li Hui bowed with joined palms in thanks and asked, "What is the Way? The Master pointed up and down and said, "Do you understand?
Li replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Clouds in the blue sky; water in the jar. Li was delighted and paid his respects, composing this verse:
"Refined is my physical form, like that of a crane; Beneath a thousand pine trees, two cases of scripture. I came to ask about the Way—no further words remain."

"Clouds in the blue sky, water in the pitcher. (See *The Record of Pointing at the Moon*, Volume Nine). "Water and fire, having attained equilibrium, accomplish the work of transformation" (*The Book of Changes*, Hexagram 63).

With the trigram Li below and Kan above, it is named "Equilibrium Attained" (*Ji Ji*). Explanation of the Principle and Image: In the blue sky, the clouds float freely; in the clear pitcher, the water remains still. This is the state of ultimate tranquility. When water and fire interact in perfect balance, they give rise to the wondrous workings of creation. As stated in the sixty-third hexagram of the *I Ching*, when the trigram of fire (Li) is below and the trigram of water (Kan) is above, it forms the hexagram "Equilibrium Attained. This signifies that all things have reached their proper fulfillment and harmony. The underlying principle is that when the forces of yin and yang are perfectly integrated, the great function of the universe unfolds. Thus, the metaphor of the cloud and the water illustrates the spontaneous and effortless perfection of the natural order.

The *Aṅguttara Nikāya* states: To the north of the great ocean, there is a great tree named Kūṭaśālmali.
This tree is one hundred yojanas high, and its branches and foliage cover fifty yojanas. Both these birds and the nāgas rely upon it.
This tree stands with four sides. The king of birds born from eggs dwells on the eastern side of the tree.

When he wishes to devour a dragon, he flies up onto the eastern branch and gazes upon the waters of the great ocean; he then immediately flies down and flaps his wings against the sea, opening it up for two hundred yojanas.
It seizes and eats dragons; this bird-king is able to seize only those born from eggs.

In this manner, up to the three types of bird-kings—those born from the womb, from moisture, and by transformation—when they wish to devour a dragon, each flies up onto a tree branch according to its respective direction and gazes upon the waters of the great ocean.
It then immediately flies down and fans the ocean water with its wings, expanding it by twice a *yojana*. Increasing the distance in sequence, it seizes the egg-born [dragons].
The four kinds of dragons—those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, and by transformation—feed upon them. The Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, there are countless species of dragons in this ocean whom the Golden-Winged Bird King constantly comes to devour.

We are terrified day and night and seek the Buddha’s protection so that we may attain peace and security. At that time, the World-Honored One immediately removed the black robe he was wearing and gave it to the dragon.
The King said, "Take these garments and distribute them among all the nāgas so that they are spread everywhere.
Even those who receive but a single thread shall be unable to commit transgressions. There was a transformed nāga youth who, on the six days of the fast, observed the eight precepts of the upavāsa.
At that time, a garuḍa, wishing to seize him for food, carried him up to the top of a great iron tree to the north of Mount Sumeru, at a height of one hundred and sixty thousand [yojanas].
He searched for its tail throughout the village but could not find it at all. Upon hearing this, the bird also received the five precepts.

As for the term "borrowed," it refers merely to matters on the periphery of form. When one cannot help but respond to the capacity of others to benefit sentient beings, this constitutes "carrying along" (xiadai).

there was a monastic friend (namely, Dao Guang) who was able to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and project his spirit (*shen*). They conversed, saying: "Today..."

Mistaking Hail for Jewels—Vainly Cherishing What Is Merely Labor.
A verse from the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* says: "For example, there was a foolish man who, seeing hail, gave rise to a deluded thought and claimed it was a lapis lazuli gem."
Having taken it up, one carries it back and places it within a vessel or container, guarding it as if it were a genuine treasure. Before long, it completely dissolves.
One then dwells in silent contemplation of emptiness. Regarding other genuine lapis lazuli as well, one likewise forms the conception of emptiness.

This brief exposition takes this as a metaphor for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who are deluded regarding the tainted heavens (*sāsrava-dhātu*) and mistake them for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet fail to recognize the fruit of true *nirvāṇa*.
