If it offends against my person, then while calamities ordained by Heaven may still be turned back, the misfortunes one brings upon oneself cannot be escaped.
Since the past, I have already defied the instructions of my teachers and guardians and failed to exercise caution from the beginning;
henceforth, I must rely on the power of righteous correction to plan for the end. This is seen in the "Tai Jia (Middle)" chapter of the Book of Shang.
Relying on the mirror to sweep away dust, there is originally not a single thing.
Great Master Shenxiu’s verse says: “The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is a stand for a bright mirror.
At all times diligently sweep and wipe it, Lest it be defiled by dust. The Sixth Patriarch Huineng’s verse says: “Bodhi is originally no tree; The bright mirror has no stand.”
Nor is it a stand; originally there was not a single thing. Where could dust and grime settle? (From the *Dharma Jewel Platform Sūtra*).
As for digging a well to a depth of nine *ren* yet failing to reach the spring, Mencius said:
"Those who engage in conditioned effort are like those who dig a well to a depth of nine *ren* (the same as *ren*) yet fail to reach the spring. It is still...
"It means 'abandoning the well. The commentary states: 'Eight chi is called a ren. This means that although the well was dug deeply, it was stopped before reaching the spring;
thus, it is like abandoning one's own well. (This is found in the "Jinxin" chapter.)

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states briefly that the Brahmin Mahākauṣṭhila, the maternal uncle of Śāriputra, was defeated in debate by his sister Śāri when they discussed the doctrine of non-appropriation (*anupādāna*).
He reflected and thought: "This is not my sister's power; she must surely harbor a wise person who has entrusted their words to her mother’s mouth. Before long—
He was born in this manner. As he grew up, he thought, "What shall I do? Having reflected thus, he gave rise to a mind of conceit.

For the sake of engaging in extensive debate, he left the household life to become a brahmin. He entered the country of South India and studied eighteen kinds of scriptures, vowing never to clip his nails;
consequently, he was known as the Long-Nail Brahmin (*Dīrghanakha*). By means of the power of his wisdom regarding various scriptures, he subdued [his opponents].
After the various masters had finished their discourse, they returned to the village of Nāla in Rājagṛha, the capital of the kingdom of Magadha, to their place of birth.
They asked the people, "Where is my sister's son now? Someone replied, "As for your sister's son—"
When he was eight years old, he had completely mastered all the scriptures. By the age of sixteen, his debating skills surpassed all others.
There was a śramaṇa of the Śākya clan named Gautama, with whom he became a disciple. When Daṇḍapāṇi heard of this, he immediately gave rise to arrogance.

He conceived a lack of faith and spoke these words: "How is it that my sister’s son, who is so intelligent, has been enticed and deceived by what sorcery into shaving his head and becoming a disciple?
Having said this, he went straight to where the Buddha was. After exchanging greetings, he sat to one side and thought:
"All arguments can be refuted; all speech can be undermined; all tenets can be overturned. Then...
When he was considering by what means of debate he might win over my sister’s son, the Buddha caused him to establish a thesis. "What is your fundamental position? the Buddha asked.

The Brahmin replied, "Gautama, my fundamental position is that I accept no doctrine whatsoever. The Buddha said, "Regarding your acceptance of no doctrine whatsoever—do you still accept this very view?
At these words, the Brahmin Dīrghanakha was like a fine horse that, upon seeing the shadow of a whip, immediately leaps forward.
He immediately realized this and entered the right path. Bowing his head, he reflected: "The Buddha has placed me between two doors of defeat.
If I were to say, 'I see and I accept,' that door of defeat would be coarse and thus known by many.
Yet now, how can I say, 'I do not accept any dharma,' while claiming 'I see and I accept'? This is a manifest falsehood; it is the second door of defeat."
[The Brahmin] said, "Subtle! I do not accept it. Having thought thus, because he did not wish for many people to know [his view], he replied to the Buddha, "Gautama, I do not accept any dharma;
I do not even accept this view. The Buddha said to the Brahmin, "If you do not accept any dharma and do not even accept this view, then you have nothing at all that is accepted.
You would be no different from the common crowd. Why then do you give rise to such arrogance?"
Due to his pride, the brahmin Dīrghanakha was unable to provide an answer. Realizing he had fallen into defeat, he immediately conceived reverence for the Buddha’s omniscience and gave rise to faith.
He entered the Buddha's order as a renunciant and realized the fruit of arhatship.
The Ancestors called this "no-mind," yet it is still separated by one further barrier.
Chan Master Tong’an Cha’s *Ten Mysterious Discourses* says: "Ask you: what is the color of the mind-seal? Who would dare to transmit the mind-seal?
Throughout kalpas it remains serene and without variation; To call it the 'mind-seal' is already a hollow word. One must know its essence..."
From the very nature of emptiness, it is likened to a lotus in a red-hot furnace. Do not say that a "mindless" state is the Way;
even mindlessness still leaves one separated by a further barrier. Thus I have seen the *Anthology of Songs and Verses of the Patriarchs of the Chan School*.
The *Jíyùn* (Collection of Clouds) states:
"The lion’s string is played amidst the myriad sounds, and all virtues converge therein. It is like a person who uses a lion’s sinew to make the strings of a lute;
when its sound is played once, all other strings are completely severed and destroyed. If a person practices the *nienfo* (recollection of the Buddha) samādhi within the bodhicitta..."
The ignorant—meaning all afflictions and all obstructions—are completely severed and extinguished.
